items.followUp: Explain how biodiversity supports food webs and nutrient cycling in a natural ecosystem.

rubric.why: Biodiversity helps keep ecosystems balanced and stable.
rubric.description: States that biodiversity supports ecosystem balance or stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that biodiversity helps maintain ecosystem balance or stability.

rubric.why: Different species are connected through feeding relationships.
rubric.description: Explains that species form food chains or food webs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning food chains or food webs.

rubric.why: Organisms contribute to recycling nutrients within ecosystems.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that biodiversity supports nutrient cycling or nutrient recycling.

rubric.why: A biodiverse ecosystem is better able to withstand or recover from environmental changes.
rubric.description: States that biodiversity increases ecosystem resilience.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that biodiversity helps an ecosystem withstand or recover from changes.

rubric.why: A specific example illustrates biodiversity's importance in a natural ecosystem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example linking forest species to pollination, food webs, or nutrient recycling.

modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in an ecosystem, and it helps maintain ecosystem balance and stability.
Different species are linked in food chains and food webs, so changes in one population can affect others.
A variety of organisms also supports essential processes such as nutrient cycling.
Biodiverse ecosystems are generally more resilient and can better withstand or recover from environmental changes.
For example, in a forest, many plant and animal species form food webs; insects pollinate plants, while decomposers recycle nutrients.

items.followUp: Explain how increasing light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affects photosynthesis, including the effect of a limiting factor.

rubric.why: Light supplies energy for photosynthesis, and greater intensity raises the rate up to a limit.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so increasing its concentration raises the rate up to a limit.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, so temperature affects its rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking temperature's effect on photosynthesis to enzymes.

rubric.why: Temperature has an optimum, and other factors can limit the rate; the rate does not increase indefinitely.
rubric.description: States the temperature limit or limiting-factor effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate decreases above the optimum temperature or levels off when another factor becomes limiting.

modelAnswer: Increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis because light supplies the energy for the process; the rate levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate because carbon dioxide is a raw material; the rate also levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum because photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes.
Above the optimum temperature, the rate decreases as the enzymes lose their proper functioning.

items.followUp: Explain what happens to a plant cell and an animal cell when they are placed in a hypotonic solution.

rubric.why: Water moves out of both cells by osmosis when they are placed in a hypertonic solution.
rubric.description: States the direction and process of water movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water leaves both cells by osmosis.

rubric.why: The animal cell loses water and shrinks because it has no cell wall.
rubric.description: Describes the effect on the animal cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the animal cell shrinks or becomes crenated.

rubric.why: Water loss makes the plant-cell protoplast contract away from the cell wall; this is plasmolysis.
rubric.description: Describes plasmolysis in the plant cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming plasmolysis or describing the protoplast pulling away from the cell wall.

rubric.why: The cell wall remains in place and helps the plant cell retain its outer shape.
rubric.description: Explains the role of the plant cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that the wall remains in place or helps retain the cell's outer shape.

rubric.why: The diagram should show the animal cell shrinking and the plant cell plasmolysed, with outward water movement and relevant labels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a diagram showing the cell outcomes and outward water movement, with suitable labels or the specified construction details.

modelAnswer: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves both plant and animal cells by osmosis.
The animal cell shrinks (crenates) because it has no cell wall to resist the loss of water.
In the plant cell, the protoplast loses water and contracts away from the cell wall; this is called plasmolysis.
The rigid cell wall remains in place and helps retain the plant cell's outer shape.
Diagram construction: draw an animal-cell circle 2 cm in diameter and a smaller, crenated outline inside it; label it “animal cell in hypertonic solution.”
Draw a plant-cell rectangle 4 cm long × 2.5 cm high; draw a smaller protoplast, about 2.5 cm × 1.2 cm, separated from the wall; label “cell wall,” “plasmolysed protoplast,” and “hypertonic solution.”
Draw at least two arrows pointing out of each cell and label them “water.”

items.followUp: Describe how the villi of the small intestine help in absorption.

rubric.why: The small intestine is located between the stomach and large intestine.
rubric.description: States the position of the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for placing it between the stomach and large intestine.

rubric.why: The small intestine is a long, coiled tube.
rubric.description: Describes the general structure of the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as a long or coiled tube.

rubric.why: Villi and microvilli increase the surface area available for absorption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning villi or microvilli and their role in increasing surface area.

rubric.why: The small intestine completes digestion and absorbs digested nutrients.
rubric.description: States the main functions of the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it completes digestion or absorbs digested nutrients.

modelAnswer: The small intestine is a long, coiled tube between the stomach and the large intestine.
Its inner lining has folds covered with many villi; the villi have microvilli that increase the surface area.
Digestive juices in the small intestine complete the digestion of food.
The digested nutrients are absorbed through the villi into the blood (and lymph).
